clinicalPearls: Combines moderate to severe intellectual disability, autism spectrum features and a distinctive epilepsy
The epilepsy is generalised, typically with myoclonic-atonic (drop) seizures, atypical absences and eyelid myoclonia often resistant to treatment
Reflex seizures triggered by eating (and sometimes by other oral or tactile stimuli) are a suggestive clue
Early hypotonia, ataxic or unsteady gait, and marked feeding and oromotor difficulties are common
Behavioural problems include autistic features, aggression, high pain threshold and disordered sleep
Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SYNGAP1, usually de novo and autosomal dominant, encoding a synaptic Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein
Language is often more impaired than expected for the overall cognitive level
reference.pathophysiology: SYNGAP1 encodes a synaptic Ras/Rap GTPase-activating protein highly enriched at excitatory glutamatergic postsynaptic densities, where it regulates AMPA-receptor trafficking and the maturation of dendritic spines. Haploinsufficiency from loss-of-function variants disturbs the balance of synaptic excitation, accelerating spine maturation and impairing synaptic plasticity underlying learning. The resulting cortical hyperexcitability and abnormal circuit development produce the intellectual disability, autistic features and generalised, frequently reflex-triggered epilepsy. The gene is dosage-sensitive, so a single functional copy is insufficient for normal synaptic function.
additionalDifferentials: Other autism spectrum disorders with epilepsy
Idiopathic generalised epilepsy with intellectual disability
additionalInvestigations: EEG, including capture during eating to document reflex seizures
Brain MRI, which is often normal or shows non-specific changes
Chromosomal microarray to detect 6p21 deletions involving SYNGAP1
Gene panel or exome sequencing for SYNGAP1 and other epileptic-encephalopathy genes
redFlags: Status epilepticus or clusters of atypical absences
Feeding difficulty with aspiration or faltering growth
Escalating aggression or self-injury affecting safety
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have lifelong intellectual disability and ongoing, often drug-resistant epilepsy, with variable but usually limited functional independence. Seizure burden and behaviour tend to be the main determinants of quality of life, and care is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Attributing the epilepsy to a generic idiopathic syndrome and not testing for SYNGAP1
Missing eating-triggered reflex seizures because EEG is not recorded around meals
Assuming a normal MRI excludes a monogenic cause
Underestimating the disproportionate language and communication impairment
management: Treat the generalised epilepsy with broad-spectrum antiseizure medication such as sodium valproate, lamotrigine, levetiracetam or ethosuximide, adding the ketogenic diet for drug-resistant seizures
Recognise and address reflex seizures triggered by eating and other oral or tactile stimuli
Provide early developmental intervention with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy and special educational support
Manage behavioural and autistic features, aggression and sleep disturbance, using melatonin for sleep, and remain alert to a high pain threshold masking injury
Support feeding and oromotor difficulties with dietetic and feeding-therapy input
Offer genetic counselling given the usually de novo, autosomal dominant, dosage-sensitive loss-of-function variants
Coordinate care through neurology, clinical genetics and neurodevelopmental services
